title: A Message for Messengers from Cush
overview: Isaiah responds to messengers from the far southern kingdom of Cush, most likely seeking allies against Assyria, by saying that God will deal with the threat in his own time and that Cush will one day honor him.

parts.label: Messengers on the Nile (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Cush was the kingdom on the upper Nile, in today's Sudan, whose kings also ruled Egypt at this time; its envoys traveled in light papyrus boats, probably seeking allies against Assyria. It is unclear who says 'Go, swift messengers': it may be Isaiah sending them home with God's answer, or Cush sending out its own envoys, and 'whirring wings' may mean buzzing insects, sails or something else.

parts.label: A signal for everyone (v. 3)
parts.note: A banner raised on a hilltop and a trumpet blast were the usual signals that war or great events were coming. The whole world is told to watch, because what God is about to do will be seen by all.

parts.label: God watches quietly (v. 4)
parts.note: God says he will wait calmly from his dwelling, as steady as summer heat or a cloud of dew at harvest. The sense seems to be that while nations scramble for alliances, God is not anxious, and his silence does not mean he is absent.

parts.label: Cut off before harvest (vv. 5-6)
parts.note: Like a vine grower cutting off shoots just before the grapes ripen, God will cut down the enemy's plans, most likely Assyria's, right before they succeed. The picture then turns grim, with the fallen left for birds and wild animals through summer and winter, which many connect with the sudden collapse of the Assyrian army outside Jerusalem told in Isaiah 37.

parts.label: Gifts brought to Zion (v. 7)
parts.note: The same tall, widely feared people from the land of rivers will one day bring gifts to the LORD at Mount Zion, the hill of Jerusalem's temple. Christians have often read this alongside the Ethiopian official in Acts 8 who traveled to Jerusalem to worship.

disagreement: Interpreters have long differed over which nation the chapter addresses: most read it as Cush on the upper Nile, but some have taken it as Egypt or even Assyria, which changes who is being warned and who brings the gifts.
think: When a frightening threat is coming, what makes it so hard to wait rather than grab at any help within reach?
